article_title: Can Videogames Be Used to Develop the Infant Stage Educational Curriculum?
citation: Marín Díaz, V.; Martín-Párraga, J. (2014). Can videogames be used to develop the infant stage educational curriculum? New Approaches in Educational Research, 3(1), 20-25. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.3.1.20-25
title: G-Learning: the educational value attributed to videogames
description: The article reports that Qasim Medhi, director of the Games Simulation and Artificial Intelligence Centre, considers the educational value added to videogames in recent times to justify the expression G-Learning. The authors note their pre-test results would initially question this statement, but found that an educational action regarding videogames can modify previous negative conceptions, so their educational value can be assumed.
requirements: Educational action or training so that teachers recognise the games' educational value
constraints: Any technology not developed with an educational aim from the beginning is not educational per se; its possibilities must be studied before it is treated as a didactic tool
target_learners: Trainee teachers and educators at any educational level
target_learning_goals: Recognising and integrating the educational value of videogames in curriculum development
key_sources: Marín Díaz, V.; Martín-Párraga, J. (2014). Can videogames be used to develop the infant stage educational curriculum? New Approaches in Educational Research, 3(1), 20-25. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.3.1.20-25

article_title: Retrospective study of online ligation student practice incorporating flipped learning into e-learning.
citation: Okada Takuhisa, Asao Takayuki, Inoue Hitoshi, Harimoto Norifumi, Tanaka Kazumi, Shiraishi Takuya, Sano Akihiko, Ogawa Hiroomi, Sohda Makoto, Shirabe Ken, Saeki Hiroshi. (2022). Retrospective study of online ligation student practice incorporating flipped learning into e-learning. Surgery Today. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00595-022-02490-y
title: G-Conference system with online ligation training videos
description: The G-Conference system is Gunma University's original web-based lecture system used for learning, mid-term checks and examinations conducted "exclusively online". It differs from existing video systems because it "can be operated using only a web browser, create user-only lecture rooms using access codes, and record lectures for review". The uploaded materials included videos from the instructor's viewpoint and videos of failure countermeasures, enabling a cycle of learning, reviewing and practicing that achieved flipped learning in an e-learning environment.
requirements: An Internet environment is needed, since the article states e-learning cannot be performed without one
Training tools (rubber bands, magnetic clips, white boards, plus surgical instruments) were distributed to each student
constraints: The creation of online training materials requires considerable effort, per the article's stated limitation
examples: Students trained "on their own time", "at their own place", and "at their own pace" over 28 days of practice, with an examination on day 19
key_sources: Okada Takuhisa, Asao Takayuki, Inoue Hitoshi, Harimoto Norifumi, Tanaka Kazumi, Shiraishi Takuya, Sano Akihiko, Ogawa Hiroomi, Sohda Makoto, Shirabe Ken, Saeki Hiroshi. (2022). Retrospective study of online ligation student practice incorporating flipped learning into e-learning. Surgery Today. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00595-022-02490-y

article_title: Reliability analysis of the objective structured clinical examination using generalizability theory.
citation: Trejo-Mejía Juan Andrés, Sánchez-Mendiola Melchor, Méndez-Ramírez Ignacio, Martínez-González Adrián. (2016). Reliability analysis of the objective structured clinical examination using generalizability theory. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v21.31650
title: Generalizability theory as a multi-facet framework for OSCE reliability analysis
description: Generalizability theory (G-theory), developed by Cronbach, models an observed score as a universal score plus multiple sources of variation called facets. Unlike Cronbach's alpha, which "estimates only one facet as a source of measurement error", G-theory "enables the calculation of multiple sources of error with a single measurement" using ANOVA techniques, yielding a G coefficient for relative reliability and a dependability (D) index for absolute reliability. In OSCEs the facets can include stations, standardized patients, examiners, scenarios/sites, and occasions.
requirements: A design defining facets and their crossing/nesting relationships (here p:sev×s)
Software able to estimate variance components for random-effects crossover and nested designs (the authors used JMP)
constraints: The article notes G-theory "is complex and requires expertise in its use"
With one examiner per station, station, examiner, and patient effects could not be separated
examples: The study applied a p:sev×s random effects design in which students were nested within site and version and crossed with station, estimating variance components for stations, sites, versions, and interactions
key_sources: Trejo-Mejía Juan Andrés, Sánchez-Mendiola Melchor, Méndez-Ramírez Ignacio, Martínez-González Adrián. (2016). Reliability analysis of the objective structured clinical examination using generalizability theory. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.3402/meo.v21.31650
